<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Note</b> </p>
  **Time:** ~10 minutes.<br>
  **Data:** a small synthetic SIRUP object included in SIRUP.

Here, we will explain the parts of a SIRUP object, the rules that SIRUP checks, and the functions that change the object.

A spatial receptor experiment gives us three kinds of data: gene expression for each spot, receptor sequences, and
regions drawn on the tissue. These data must agree with each other. For example, a receptor must belong to a spot that exists,
and a clone column must exist in the receptor table. The SIRUP object keeps all of the data in one place and checks these rules
each time the object changes.

<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Note</b> </p>
  This page has little code. To build an object from real data, see `vignette("get-started", package = "SIRUP")` first.
</div>

## Load the example object

The examples use a small synthetic object with 25 spots, 10 genes, 5 clones, and 2 polygons. The spots and gene counts
are simulated. The receptor rows are real BCR sequences from a human thymus section, assigned to synthetic spots.

```{r load}
library(SIRUP)

x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
x
```

## Look at the five parts of the object

A SIRUP object is a list with five parts, in this order:

| Part | Contents | How to get it |
|---|---|---|
| `spatial` | The Seurat object, with expression and the H&E image | `getSpatial(x)` |
| `receptors` | The AIRR receptor table, as a tibble, or a named list of tables | `getReceptors(x)` |
| `metadata` | The field names and the image settings | `x$metadata` |
| `polygons` | The tissue regions, with one row for each polygon | `getPolygons(x)` |
| `analyses` | Results that are saved in the object | `getAnalysis(x, name)` |

The accessors return ordinary R objects, so they can be passed to any function from another package.

```{r parts}
getSpatial(x)
head(getReceptors(x), 3)
getPolygons(x)
```

`summary()` gives counts for each part:

```{r summary}
summary(x)
```

## Set the field names

A receptor table can use any column names, so SIRUP needs to know which column plays which role. It stores this map
in `x$metadata$receptor_fields`. There are six fields:

| Field | The receptor column that holds... |
|---|---|
| `spatial_id` | the name of the spot that holds the receptor |
| `image` | the name of the Seurat image, if the object has several images |
| `sample` | the sample name, in a multi-sample object |
| `clone` | the clone ID |
| `locus` | the receptor locus, such as `IGH` or `TRB` |
| `count` | the number of reads or UMIs of the sequence |

```{r fields}
x$metadata$receptor_fields
```

The fields are set once, in `createSIRUP()`. After that, SIRUP functions find each column without extra arguments. To change a field later,
give a new map to `updateReceptors()` with the `receptor_fields` argument. A value of `NULL` clears an optional field.

## Validate the object

`validateSIRUP()` checks that the parts agree. It gives an error if one of these rules fails:

1. The object has class `sirup`.
2. At least one receptor spatial ID matches a spot name in the Seurat object.
3. Each column that `receptor_fields` names exists in the receptor table. If the object has several receptor tables, the spatial ID
   column must be in every table. Each other named column, such as `clone_id`, must be in at least one table.
4. If the sample field is set, the column exists in every receptor table and in the Seurat metadata.

```{r validate}
validateSIRUP(x, verbose = TRUE)
```

`createSIRUP()`, `updateReceptors()`, `updateSpatial()`, and the other functions that change the object run this check before they
return. A change that breaks a rule fails right away and leaves the original object as it was. This example gives every receptor a
spot name that does not exist:

```{r broken}
tryCatch(
  updateReceptors(x, function(receptors) {
    receptors$spatial_id <- "no-such-spot"
    receptors
  }),
  error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)
)
```

<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Note</b> </p>
  SIRUP keeps receptor rows that match no spot, such as bulk and blood sequences. The rules need only one match, so these rows stay in the table.
</div>

## Set the image settings

Two settings tell SIRUP how to put spots on the H&E image. Both are stored in `x$metadata`:

* `image_scale` is the Seurat image scale, `"lowres"` or `"hires"`.
* `swap_coords` swaps the x and y coordinates. Some older Seurat objects store the coordinates in the opposite order to the image.

Plots and spatial statistics read these settings when their own `image_scale` and `swap_coords` arguments are `NULL`, so
they only need to be set once.

## Change the data in the object

SIRUP does not wrap every AIRR tool. Instead, three functions run any function on one part of the object and put the result back:

* `updateReceptors(x, fun, ...)` calls `fun(getReceptors(x), ...)` and stores the table that `fun` returns.
* `updateSpatial(x, fun, ...)` calls `fun(getSpatial(x), ...)` and stores the Seurat object that `fun` returns.
* `updateAnalysis(x, name, fun, ...)` does the same for a stored analysis.

Each function validates the object again before it returns. This call removes the sequences of one clone:

```{r update-receptors}
x2 <- updateReceptors(x, dplyr::filter, clone_id != "3")
c(before = nrow(getReceptors(x)), after = nrow(getReceptors(x2)))
```

This call adds a column to the Seurat metadata:

```{r update-spatial}
x3 <- updateSpatial(x, function(spatial) {
  spatial$gene_rich <- spatial$nFeature_Spatial >= 8
  spatial
})
table(getSpatial(x3)$gene_rich)
```

The same pattern runs germline reconstruction (`dowser::createGermlines()`) or mutation counting (`shazam::observedMutations()`) inside the
object. `vignette("clones-and-trees", package = "SIRUP")` shows these steps.

## Add regions to the object

A region is a polygon on the tissue image. `addPolygons()` stores the polygons and then marks the polygon of each spot and each receptor.
It adds a `polygon_id` column and one logical `polygon_<ID>` column for each polygon to both the Seurat metadata and the receptor table.

```{r polygon-columns}
grep("^polygon", names(getReceptors(x)), value = TRUE)
grep("^polygon", names(getSpatial(x)[[]]), value = TRUE)
```

A spot on the edge of a polygon counts as a member when `include_boundary` is `TRUE`, which is the default.
`vignette("regions", package = "SIRUP")` shows how to draw regions and measure what they hold.

## Hold several receptor tables

One object can hold more than one receptor table, e.g., one table of BCRs and one of TCRs. Give `createSIRUP()` a named list of tables.
Each table is a *slot*. All slots share the spatial data, the polygons, and the field names. The spatial ID column must be in every table,
but a column such as `clone_id` can be in one table only, e.g., the BCR table. Clone IDs only need to be unique within one slot.

```{r slots}
bcr <- getReceptors(x)
tcr <- bcr[1:8, ]
tcr$locus <- "TRB"

both <- createSIRUP(
  spatial = getSpatial(x),
  receptors = list(bcr = bcr, tcr = tcr),
  spatial_id = "spatial_id",
  clone = "clone_id",
  image_scale = "hires",
  swap_coords = FALSE,
  polygons = getPolygons(x)
)
receptorSlots(both)
both
```

Functions that use receptors work on one slot at a time, chosen with the `slot` argument. If the object has several slots, `slot` is
required. If the object has one table, leave it out. That table has the slot name `"only_slot"`.

```{r slot-use}
head(getReceptors(both, slot = "tcr"), 3)
both <- polygonReceptorSummary(both, slot = "tcr")
listAnalyses(both)
tryCatch(getReceptors(both), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

The polygons apply to every slot. A receptor is in a polygon if it is in the same sample and its spatial ID lies inside the polygon.
The default analysis names end with the slot name, so results for different slots do not overwrite each other.

## Hold several samples

`createSIRUP()` accepts one Seurat object or a named list of Seurat objects, e.g., one for each tissue section. With a list, the column of the receptor table that `sample_id` names matches each row
to a list entry. Rows with no matching entry stay in the table as non-spatial records, which is how bulk and blood sequences are stored. Spot barcodes can repeat between sections, so SIRUP matches
each receptor to a spot by the pair of sample and barcode.

```{r samples}
receptors <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::mutate(getReceptors(x), sample = "a"),
  dplyr::mutate(getReceptors(x), sample = "b")
)

two_samples <- createSIRUP(
  spatial = list(a = getSpatial(x), b = getSpatial(x)),
  receptors = receptors,
  spatial_id = "spatial_id",
  clone = "clone_id",
  sample_id = "sample",
  image_scale = "hires",
  swap_coords = FALSE
)
two_samples
spatialSamples(two_samples)
```

If the sections need different image settings, give named values, e.g., `image_scale = c(a = "hires", b = "lowres")`.

`mergeSIRUP()` goes the other way. It joins several single-sample objects into one, with the sample names that are given:

```{r merge}
merged <- mergeSIRUP(x, x, samples = c("a", "b"), sample_field = "sample")
spatialSamples(merged)
```

`subsetSIRUP()` keeps chosen samples, spots, or receptor rows. `getSpatial()` and `getReceptors()` return the data of one sample when `sample_id` is given.
`vignette("multisample", package = "SIRUP")` has a full example.

## Save results in the object

`setAnalysis()` stores any R object under a name, e.g., clones, trees, spatial statistics, and polygon summaries. Stored results stay with the data
that made them, so separate files do not need to be tracked.

```{r analyses}
x <- setAnalysis(x, "n_clones", 5)
listAnalyses(x)
getAnalysis(x, "n_clones")
x <- removeAnalysis(x, "n_clones")
listAnalyses(x)
```

## Save and read a SIRUP object

`saveSIRUP()` validates the object and writes it to one RDS file. The file also records the versions of SIRUP and SeuratObject that wrote it.
`readSIRUP()` reads the file and does four things. It converts an object saved under the old package name (SIRAP), upgrades an older object to
the current layout, warns if the package versions differ from the file, and validates the object.

```{r save-read}
path <- saveSIRUP(x, tempfile(fileext = ".sirup.rds"))
x_again <- readSIRUP(path)
x_again
```
